data.title: PoL Probe: do conflicts when merging tasks happen at all
body: # PoL Probe: do conflicts when merging tasks happen at all
- **Owner:** the project's author
- **Hypothesis under test:** assumption #1 from the [map](DOC-39) — Risk 8.0
## Why not interviews first

The template proposes interviews for value assumptions. For a solo developer with no budget and no ready network of interviewees that is 2–3 weeks of recruiting, and what comes out is people's opinions about how often they have conflicts. Memory of such events is unreliable: a small conflict is resolved in a minute and forgotten.

But this hypothesis can be tested **with facts rather than recollections**. Backlog.md and git-issues are already used in public repositories. Their tasks are files in git. So the merge history of those files is available to read.
Asking people whether they have conflicts, when the conflicts can be counted, is choosing the worse source of truth.
## Probe A — git archaeology (first)
**Type:** Feasibility Check / analysis of existing data
**Question:** do conflicts happen in task files in real projects that already live on file-based trackers?
**Method**
1. Find 30–50 public repositories with a `backlog/` or `.issues/` directory and more than 3 months of activity.
2. For each, go through the merge commits of the last half-year and count:
- merges that touched task files;
- among them, those that had a conflict (traces of resolution in the merge commit);
- separately, ID collisions (two branches created a task with the same number — exactly what their `task-4.12` is about).
3. Count the share of conflicting merges per repository per month.
**Thresholds, set before the start**
- **Hypothesis confirmed:** conflicts in task files in more than 30% of active repositories, or more often than once a month in the median repository.
- **Hypothesis dead:** fewer than 10% of repositories had even one such conflict in half a year. Then append-only solves a problem that does not exist in nature, and the product's main thesis falls.
- **Ambiguous:** between 10% and 30% → we move on to Probe B.
**Cost:** 1 day. **Disposal:** the script is deleted, the table of numbers remains.

**An honest limitation:** the absence of conflicts may mean not "there is no problem" but "people avoid it by working one at a time". For the product the consequence is the same — the pain is not felt. But for the wording of the conclusion the difference matters, and that is exactly what Probe B establishes.
## Probe B — interviews (if Probe A is ambiguous)
**Type:** Task-Focused / problem interviews
**Question:** if conflicts are rare — does a pain exist that is worth changing tools for?
The script is in [interview-script.md](DOC-49). 5–7 interviewees.
**Thresholds**
- **Confirmed:** at least 4 of 7 give a concrete case from the last 3 months **and** describe what they did next.
- **Dead:** the majority say "yes, it's annoying", but not one mentions a concrete case. General agreement without a story is politeness, not data.
**Cost:** 3–5 days including recruiting.
## Probe C — fake doors (in parallel, almost free)
**Question:** what catches the audience — conflicts or velocity?
Two pages with identical functionality and different headlines:
- A: "Tasks in the repo that do not conflict on merge"
- B: "Your team's velocity, counted from git history"
Hand them out in the same channels, compare the share of those who get as far as "try it".
**Threshold:** a difference of less than one and a half times — neither message is strong, and the problem is in the positioning, not in the text.
**An honest limitation:** without traffic this will be a dozen clicks. Treat it as a direction, not as statistics.
## The order and what it decides
| | Probe | Days | What it closes |
| 1 | A — git archaeology | 1 | Whether the problem exists **in nature** |
| 2 | C — fake doors | 1 + waiting | Which message catches at all |
| 3 | B — interviews | 3–5 | Whether it hurts enough to change tools |

**Probe A has to be first, and it can close the project in a single day.** That is its main value: if 50 repositories have no conflicts in task files over half a year — no interview will save the thesis any more, and it is better to learn that before writing the code than after.
## The disposal rule

Everything written for a probe is deleted after it. Only the numbers and the conclusion remain. If some script feels worth "keeping, because it will come in handy" — that is a signal that the probe has stopped being a probe.
